interpretations.rationale: The conclusion is a violated requirement and a bounded client-completion defect for remote ReadIndex requests whenever the leader confirms a later queued context before an earlier one. The source cause is that handleReadIndexLeaderConfirmation returns every earlier queued request but builds each remote reply from the confirming heartbeat's Hint and HintHigh instead of that request's s.ctx, while readIndex.confirm deletes the earlier queue entry and the receiving node's pendingReadIndex associates a batch only when the response SystemCtx equals the registered key. That ordering needs no artificial message reordering: while a read is pending, the leader's periodic heartbeat carries the newest queued context because peepCtx returns the last queued context, followers echo the hint, and handleLeaderHeartbeatResp confirms it, so a confirmation produced by a periodic heartbeat confirms the newest pending request and returns every earlier queued request under that context. The receipts cover four requesters and both a harness-chosen and a tick-driven confirmation. In the follower receipt, node 2's admitted context {101,1002} is answered with node 3's later context {202,2003} at log index 4, and node 2's batch stays at index zero after the real ready index 4 is applied; the late confirmation of node 2's own context produces no context-correct reply. The logical-deadline receipt keeps that ordering and shows no completion before the 50-tick deadline, RequestTimeout at tick 51, and removal of the stale batch. The observer-endpoint receipt closes the link that the earlier leader-side observer receipt left open: a real observer peer forwards its own generated context to the real leader, voter 3's later context is confirmed first, the reply addressed to observer 4 carries voter 3's context at log index 4, the observer's real handler emits a ReadyToRead carrying that later context at index 4, and the observer's admitted batch stays at index zero without completing, even after the late own-context confirmation. The tick-driven receipt shows the same substitution under ordinary operation instead of harness-selected delivery: with two queued follower reads, one leader tick makes the periodic heartbeat carry the newest context, the reply to the earlier requester carries that newest context at index 4, and its batch stays at index zero. The shared-confirmation receipt locates the fault within the reply construction rather than in confirmation or index selection: one broadcast carrying the later local context returns an earlier remote read and the later leader-local read, the local requester's ready-to-read result carries its own context and completes at index 4, and the remote requester is answered with the local context and stays at index zero. The multi-requester receipt widens that from one stranded request to a batch: with three remote reads queued from two nodes and one tick-driven confirmation, the earliest and middle requests stay at index zero while only the newest completes, so one node's later read succeeds while its own earlier read does not. The three controls complete when the admitted context is confirmed first or is the only queued context: the follower control's reply carries its context and its read completes at batch index 4, the observer control's reply carries the observer's context and its read completes, and the single-read tick control carries that read's own context and completes at batch index 4.  The repair implied by the measured branch is local to that send: build the ReadIndexResp for each returned readStatus from that status's own ctx instead of the confirming heartbeat's Hint and HintHigh, leaving confirm, the queue deletion and the receiving node's exact-key association unchanged; no repair was applied or tested here. Because every measured reply carries a later committed index and the ready index equals the applied index, no stale read value or safety violation is established; the established consequence is that an affected client read cannot complete until its deadline even though the leader had a completed confirmation and the node applied a valid ready index. The observer case shows the defect reaches a non-voting client endpoint through the observer's own forwarding and consumer rather than only the leader's outbound message.

interpretations.rationale: The suspicion is refuted for the captured legal paths, although the low-level code alone would count it. handleLeaderHeartbeatResp confirms when a heartbeat response carries a nonzero hint, lw admits observer responses, and readIndex.confirm counts the responding node without checking whether it is currently a voter. That is the plausible weakness. The legal transition path does not create the needed state: membership rejects AddObserver or AddWitness for a current address; RemoveNode deletes the node from remotes, observers, and witnesses and marks it removed; isAddRemovedNode rejects re-adding that ID as any role; and raft.restore panics if a non-observer or non-witness local node appears in the snapshot's observer or witness set. In addition, broadcastHeartbeatMessageWithHint sends nonzero-context heartbeats only to votingMembers and sends observer heartbeats only for the zero context. A delayed response from a removed voter is therefore ignored because lw no longer finds it in any role map, and a delayed nonzero context cannot come from an observer under legal transitions. The rejoining-as-observer path is blocked by membership. The conclusion is a protective-mechanism negative result, not a claim that arbitrary direct map mutation or a malicious observer is safe; those are outside the admitted scenario and would still expose the low-level counting behavior.

interpretations.rationale: The suspicion is refuted for the captured raft paths. The hazard requires a leader whose log holds a committed configuration change that its membership maps have not yet applied, because tryCommit computes the quorum from those maps and a second change committed before the first is applied would be committed with the pre-change quorum. Two gates prevent that history. A leader that proposed a configuration change sets pendingConfigChange in handleLeaderPropose and keeps it set until a configuration-change apply path clears it, so any further configuration change it proposes is reported dropped and replaced with an empty application entry; the leader cannot accumulate a second uncommitted change while the first is committed but unapplied. A node that did not propose the change can only become leader by campaigning, and handleNodeElection refuses to campaign while log.committed exceeds the applied index, so a node that still has any committed unapplied entry, including a configuration change, cannot become leader; TimeoutNow cannot bypass this because it only advances the election tick and lets the normal tick emit the Election message that handleNodeElection gates. preLeaderPromotionHandleConfigChange therefore runs only after the applied index has caught up with the committed index, and its count of entries after the committed index is consistent with that state; it re-sets the pending flag for the single uncommitted change it can legitimately find and panics if the log ever holds more than one. The consequence is an availability tradeoff rather than the suspected safety violation: while the applied index lags, the node declines to campaign, and a leader keeps dropping configuration changes until the in-flight change is applied. The low-level pieces that suggested the hazard remain exactly as described, but the permitted leadership and proposal histories do not produce the required state.
counterevidence: getPendingConfigChangeCount starts at the committed index plus one, so a committed but unapplied configuration change is never counted as pending, and pendingConfigChange is a single boolean that does not record which change it tracks.

tryCommit computes the quorum from the raft membership maps, which the apply paths change only when a configuration change is applied, so the hazard would be real if a leader could accept a second change before the first was applied.

interpretations.rationale: The suspicion that a granted vote could be lost before the vote response is sent is refuted for the captured batch path. processSteps takes one update per active node, emits only the messages that isFreeOrderMessage classifies as free order, which is Replicate and Ping, and then calls SaveRaftState for the whole batch; the log DB contract says that call atomically saves the raft states, log entries and snapshot metadata, and the implementation puts each non-empty state and the entries into one write batch that it commits once. interpretations.rationale: The suspicion is refuted for the captured restore paths. raft.restore first rejects a snapshot whose index does not exceed the committed index, so a stale snapshot cannot move the log backward, and it refuses to convert the local node into an observer or witness. When the snapshot is accepted, the log sets its committed and processed positions to the snapshot index, and restoreRemotes then rebuilds all three role maps from the snapshot membership with fresh map allocations rather than merging them, so a node absent from the snapshot is no longer present in remotes, observers or witnesses and cannot be counted in a later quorum; a leader that the snapshot removes steps down. The running-follower path reaches that replacement indirectly: the node applies the snapshot to its logs and schedules a Recover task, and the state machine calls RestoreRemotes for that snapshot when it runs the task. During the interval between the log restore and that task, the raft committed index already equals the snapshot index while the applied index still lags, and handleNodeElection refuses to campaign while the committed index exceeds the applied index, so the node cannot use the interim membership to start an election. The remaining exposure is the supervisor's own ordering rather than a raft merge: the membership maps are replaced only when the state machine completes Recover, which the captured code schedules immediately after applying the snapshot.

interpretations.rationale: The conclusion is a violated requirement and a bounded client-completion defect for remote ReadIndex requests whenever the leader confirms a later queued context before an earlier one. The source cause is that handleReadIndexLeaderConfirmation returns every earlier queued request but builds each remote reply from the confirming heartbeat's Hint and HintHigh instead of that request's s.ctx, while readIndex.confirm deletes the earlier queue entry and the receiving node's pendingReadIndex associates a batch only when the response SystemCtx equals the registered key. That ordering needs no artificial message reordering: while a read is pending, the leader's periodic heartbeat carries the newest queued context because peepCtx returns the last queued context, followers echo the hint, and handleLeaderHeartbeatResp confirms it, so a confirmation produced by a periodic heartbeat confirms the newest pending request and returns every earlier queued request under that context. The receipts cover four requesters and both a harness-chosen and a tick-driven confirmation. In the follower receipt, node 2's admitted context {101,1002} is answered with node 3's later context {202,2003} at log index 4, and node 2's batch stays at index zero after the real ready index 4 is applied; the late confirmation of node 2's own context produces no context-correct reply. The logical-deadline receipt keeps that ordering and shows no completion before the 50-tick deadline, RequestTimeout at tick 51, and removal of the stale batch. The observer-endpoint receipt closes the link that the earlier leader-side observer receipt left open: a real observer peer forwards its own generated context to the real leader, voter 3's later context is confirmed first, the reply addressed to observer 4 carries voter 3's context at log index 4, the observer's real handler emits a ReadyToRead carrying that later context at index 4, and the observer's admitted batch stays at index zero without completing, even after the late own-context confirmation. interpretations.rationale: The suspicion is refuted for the captured raft paths. The hazard requires a leader whose log holds a committed configuration change that its membership maps have not yet applied, because tryCommit computes the quorum from those maps and a second change committed before the first is applied would be committed with the pre-change quorum. Two gates prevent that history. A leader that proposed a configuration change sets pendingConfigChange in handleLeaderPropose and keeps it set until a configuration-change apply path clears it, so any further configuration change it proposes is reported dropped and replaced with an empty application entry; the leader cannot accumulate a second uncommitted change while the first is committed but unapplied. A node that did not propose the change can only become leader by campaigning, and handleNodeElection refuses to campaign while log.committed exceeds the applied index, so a node that still has any committed unapplied entry, including a configuration change, cannot become leader; TimeoutNow cannot bypass this because it only advances the election tick and lets the normal tick emit the Election message that handleNodeElection gates. preLeaderPromotionHandleConfigChange therefore runs only after the applied index has caught up with the committed index, and its count of entries after the committed index is consistent with that state; it re-sets the pending flag for the single uncommitted change it can legitimately find and panics if the log ever holds more than one. The consequence is an availability tradeoff rather than the suspected safety violation: while the applied index lags, the node declines to campaign, and a leader keeps dropping configuration changes until the in-flight change is applied. The low-level pieces that suggested the hazard remain exactly as described, but the permitted leadership and proposal histories do not produce the required state.
counterevidence: getPendingConfigChangeCount starts at the committed index plus one, so a committed but unapplied configuration change is never counted as pending, and pendingConfigChange is a single boolean that does not record which change it tracks.

tryCommit computes the quorum from the raft membership maps, which the apply paths change only when a configuration change is applied, so the hazard would be real if a leader could accept a second change before the first was applied.

The election gate is a general committed-versus-applied comparison, so the refutation depends on the applied index being advanced only after the state machine has applied those entries, which is the value node.updateAppliedIndex forwards.
limitations: This is a source-only account; no execution of the leadership, proposal or apply ordering is retained for it.

Direct mutation of the internal role maps, an operator starting a node with a role inconsistent with cluster membership, forged messages, and a custom transport that changes message admission are excluded.
The gate is a liveness tradeoff: a node whose applied index lags cannot campaign and a leader keeps dropping configuration changes, and no bound on that delay is established.
Snapshot restore and configuration changes carried by snapshots are covered only by the role guards recorded elsewhere, not by this account.

interpretations.rationale: The suspicion that a granted vote could be lost before the vote response is sent is refuted for the captured batch path. processSteps takes one update per active node, emits only the messages that isFreeOrderMessage classifies as free order, which is Replicate and Ping, and then calls SaveRaftState for the whole batch; the log DB contract says that call atomically saves the raft states, log entries and snapshot metadata, and the implementation puts each non-empty state and the entries into one write batch that it commits once. The remaining messages travel in the same update through processRaftUpdate, which runs only after that commit, so RequestVoteResp, HeartbeatResp, ReplicateResp and ReadIndexResp are all emitted after the state that justifies them is durable. A crash after a vote response therefore cannot leave the previous vote or term in place, and the node cannot grant a different vote in the same term. The pre-persistence Replicate and Ping emission is the deliberate exception documented at the call site with a reference to section 10.2.1 of the Raft thesis; those messages carry no granted authority of their own, so the ordering that matters for election safety is preserved. The refutation covers the ordering of the local atomic write batch, not the durability guarantees of a specific storage engine.

knowledge.assertion: Non-free-order messages, including RequestVoteResp and HeartbeatResp, are forwarded only after the batch's raft state has been committed atomically.

counterevidence: The free-order exception sends Replicate and Ping before persistence, so the ordering guarantee applies to the messages that carry votes, heartbeats and read replies, not to those two message types.

The peer includes a raft state in the update only when it differs from the previously committed state, so the guarantee depends on that difference being reported for the step in which the vote changed.
The guarantee is about the log DB's atomic write batch; a storage layer that acknowledged the batch without making it durable would defeat it, and that layer is outside the captured source.

interpretations.rationale: The suspicion is refuted for the captured raft paths. The hazard requires a leader whose log holds a committed configuration change that its membership maps have not yet applied, because tryCommit computes the quorum from those maps and a second change committed before the first is applied would be committed with the pre-change quorum. Two gates prevent that history. A leader that proposed a configuration change sets pendingConfigChange in handleLeaderPropose and keeps it set until a configuration-change apply path clears it, so any further configuration change it proposes is reported dropped and replaced with an empty application entry; the leader cannot accumulate a second uncommitted change while the first is committed but unapplied. That gate is now measured at a live leader: an AddNode for node 4 was saved as a configuration-change entry, and an AddNode for node 5 proposed before the first was committed or applied was saved as a plain application entry and reported dropped under its own key. A node that did not propose the change can only become leader by campaigning, and handleNodeElection refuses to campaign while log.committed exceeds the applied index, so a node that still has any committed unapplied entry, including a configuration change, cannot become leader; TimeoutNow cannot bypass this because it only advances the election tick and lets the normal tick emit the Election message that handleNodeElection gates. preLeaderPromotionHandleConfigChange therefore runs only after the applied index has caught up with the committed index, and its count of entries after the committed index is consistent with that state; it re-sets the pending flag for the single uncommitted change it can legitimately find and panics if the log ever holds more than one. The consequence is an availability tradeoff rather than the suspected safety violation: while the applied index lags, the node declines to campaign, and a leader keeps dropping configuration changes until the in-flight change is applied. The low-level pieces that suggested the hazard remain exactly as described, but the permitted leadership and proposal histories do not produce the required state.

That ordering needs no artificial message reordering: while a read is pending, the leader's periodic heartbeat carries the newest queued context because peepCtx returns the last queued context, followers echo the hint, and handleLeaderHeartbeatResp confirms it, so a confirmation produced by a periodic heartbeat confirms the newest pending request and returns every earlier queued request under that context. The receipts cover four requesters and both a harness-chosen and a tick-driven confirmation. In the follower receipt, node 2's admitted context {101,1002} is answered with node 3's later context {202,2003} at log index 4, and node 2's batch stays at index zero after the real ready index 4 is applied; the late confirmation of node 2's own context produces no context-correct reply. The logical-deadline receipt keeps that ordering and shows no completion before the 50-tick deadline, RequestTimeout at tick 51, and removal of the stale batch. The observer-endpoint receipt closes the link that the earlier leader-side observer receipt left open: a real observer peer forwards its own generated context to the real leader, voter 3's later context is confirmed first, the reply addressed to observer 4 carries voter 3's context at log index 4, the observer's real handler emits a ReadyToRead carrying that later context at index 4, and the observer's admitted batch stays at index zero without completing, even after the late own-context confirmation. The tick-driven receipt shows the same substitution under ordinary operation instead of harness-selected delivery: with two queued follower reads, one leader tick makes the periodic heartbeat carry the newest context, the reply to the earlier requester carries that newest context at index 4, and its batch stays at index zero. The shared-confirmation receipt locates the fault within the reply construction rather than in confirmation or index selection: one broadcast carrying the later local context returns an earlier remote read and the later leader-local read, the local requester's ready-to-read result carries its own context and completes at index 4, and the remote requester is answered with the local context and stays at index zero. The multi-requester receipt widens that from one stranded request to a batch: with three remote reads queued from two nodes and one tick-driven confirmation, the earliest and middle requests stay at index zero while only the newest completes, so one node's later read succeeds while its own earlier read does not. The three controls complete when the admitted context is confirmed first or is the only queued context: the follower control's reply carries its context and its read completes at batch index 4, the observer control's reply carries the observer's context and its read completes, and the single-read tick control carries that read's own context and completes at batch index 4. Because every measured reply carries a later committed index and the ready index equals the applied index, no stale read value or safety violation is established; the established consequence is that an affected client read cannot complete until its deadline even though the leader had a completed confirmation and the node applied a valid ready index. The observer case shows the defect reaches a non-voting client endpoint through the observer's own forwarding and consumer rather than only the leader's outbound message.

interpretations.rationale: The captured source locates the client surface of the parent question's asserted defect. NodeHost.SyncRead passes the caller context to linearizableRead, which reaches the internal readIndex helper and node.read; node.read registers the read through pendingReadIndex.read and returns the RequestState, and the helper marks the node ready so the read is sent. NodeHost.ReadIndex, the API documented for the two-step pattern, calls the same helper and returns that RequestState, and ReadLocalNode guards on the ready-to-read flag that only a completed batch sets. The wait path maps results uniformly: a completed result returns normally, a timeout result or an expired caller context returns ErrTimeout, a dropped result returns ErrClusterNotReady, and rejected, terminated or aborted results map to their own errors. Combined with the parent receipts, in which a reply carrying another request's context left the admitted batch at index zero after a valid ready index was applied, the client-visible endpoint for an affected follower or observer read is ErrTimeout at the caller's deadline rather than a completion, and it is distinguishable from the dropped path that returns ErrClusterNotReady. This account is source-only and makes no independent defect claim; the defect judgment and its receipts remain in the parent question.

interpretations.rationale: The conclusion is a violated requirement and a bounded client-completion defect for remote ReadIndex requests whenever the leader confirms a later queued context before an earlier one. The source cause is that handleReadIndexLeaderConfirmation returns every earlier queued request but builds each remote reply from the confirming heartbeat's Hint and HintHigh instead of that request's s.ctx, while readIndex.confirm deletes the earlier queue entry and the receiving node's pendingReadIndex associates a batch only when the response SystemCtx equals the registered key. That ordering needs no artificial message reordering: while a read is pending, the leader's periodic heartbeat carries the newest queued context because peepCtx returns the last queued context, followers echo the hint, and handleLeaderHeartbeatResp confirms it, so a confirmation produced by a periodic heartbeat confirms the newest pending request and returns every earlier queued request under that context. The receipts cover four requesters and both a harness-chosen and a tick-driven confirmation. In the follower receipt, node 2's admitted context {101,1002} is answered with node 3's later context {202,2003} at log index 4, and node 2's batch stays at index zero after the real ready index 4 is applied; the late confirmation of node 2's own context produces no context-correct reply. The logical-deadline receipt keeps that ordering and shows no completion before the 50-tick deadline, RequestTimeout at tick 51, and removal of the stale batch. The observer-endpoint receipt closes the link that the earlier leader-side observer receipt left open: a real observer peer forwards its own generated context to the real leader, voter 3's later context is confirmed first, the reply addressed to observer 4 carries voter 3's context at log index 4, the observer's real handler emits a ReadyToRead carrying that later context at index 4, and the observer's admitted batch stays at index zero without completing, even after the late own-context confirmation. The tick-driven receipt shows the same substitution under ordinary operation instead of harness-selected delivery: with two queued follower reads, one leader tick makes the periodic heartbeat carry the newest context, the reply to the earlier requester carries that newest context at index 4, and its batch stays at index zero. The shared-confirmation receipt locates the fault within the reply construction rather than in confirmation or index selection: one broadcast carrying the later local context returns an earlier remote read and the later leader-local read, the local requester's ready-to-read result carries its own context and completes at index 4, and the remote requester is answered with the local context and stays at index zero.
